title: Breathing and gas exchange
blurb: Explain how pressure changes move air in and out, how lung volumes add up, and how O₂ and CO₂ cross the respiratory membrane and travel in the blood.
question: As a patient breathes in, the diaphragm contracts. Which way does it move, why does air flow in, and once the air reaches the alveoli, how do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross into and out of the blood?

teach.h: Air always flows from high to low pressure
teach.body: Formally, pulmonary ventilation is the movement of air into and out of the lungs, driven by pressure differences. It follows Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely related. In plain English: make the chest bigger and the pressure inside drops, so outside air rushes in; make the chest smaller and the pressure rises, so air is pushed out.

teach.caption: Quiet breathing out at rest relies on elastic recoil. Muscles only join in when you blow out forcefully.

teach.h: The diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing
teach.body: The dome-shaped diaphragm, supplied by the phrenic nerve, does most of the work of quiet breathing. When it contracts it flattens and moves down, lengthening the chest cavity. The lungs follow the chest wall because pleural fluid holds the two pleural layers together. When the diaphragm relaxes, it rises back into its dome and the lungs recoil. Normal adult resting rate is about 12 to 20 breaths per minute.

teach.caption: Note the dome of the diaphragm under the lungs: it contracts and flattens downward on inspiration, enlarging the chest so air flows in.
Worked example: TV 500 mL + IRV 2,800 mL + ERV 1,200 mL = VC 4,500 mL; add RV 1,300 mL for TLC 5,800 mL. Residual volume is in TLC but never in VC.

teach.h: Gas exchange: down the partial-pressure gradient
teach.body: Formally, external respiration is gas exchange between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries; internal respiration is exchange between systemic capillaries and tissue cells. Both happen by simple diffusion: each gas moves from higher to lower partial pressure, with no ATP. The respiratory membrane (alveolar wall plus capillary wall) is very thin. Plain English: O₂ loads in the lungs and unloads in the tissues; CO₂ does the reverse.

teach.caption: Cellular respiration (making ATP in mitochondria) is a third, different process.

head: Gas
Main form
Minor forms
teach.caption: Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more strongly than O₂.

teach.body: Priya, a nursing applicant, breathes fast and deep during a panic attack before her HESI A2. Rising CO₂ is normally the main drive to breathe, sensed in the medulla oblongata, which sets the rhythm. By overbreathing she blows off CO₂, the bicarbonate reaction shifts left, H⁺ falls and her blood pH rises: respiratory alkalosis. Slow, shallow breathing would do the opposite: CO₂ builds up and pH falls (respiratory acidosis).

teach.text: The diaphragm moves DOWN (flattens) when you breathe in, and quiet expiration is PASSIVE. Residual volume is in total lung capacity but NOT vital capacity. O₂ travels mostly BOUND TO HEMOGLOBIN, not dissolved; CO₂ travels mostly as BICARBONATE, not on hemoglobin.

items: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, gas pressure and volume are inversely related.
Inspiration is active (diaphragm down, external intercostals); quiet expiration is passive recoil.
Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV; total lung capacity = VC + RV.
Gas exchange is simple diffusion down partial-pressure gradients: external in the lungs, internal in the tissues.
O₂ mostly on hemoglobin; CO₂ mostly as bicarbonate (carbonic anhydrase in RBCs).

summary: You can now explain breathing with Boyle's law, name the muscles of inspiration and forced expiration, and calculate vital capacity and total lung capacity. You can also describe external and internal respiration as diffusion down partial-pressure gradients and state how blood carries O₂ and CO₂.

A.q: During a normal, quiet inspiration, what does the diaphragm do?
A.why: The diaphragm contracts, flattening and moving down. This enlarges the thoracic cavity so lung pressure falls and air flows in.

whyNot.1: A relaxing diaphragm rises back into its dome; it does not sink down.
whyNot.2: Contraction flattens the diaphragm downward. Bulging up would shrink the chest and push air out.
whyNot.3: Relaxing and rising is what happens during expiration, not inspiration.

A.q: By Boyle's law, when the volume of the thoracic cavity increases, the pressure inside the lungs:
options: Rises, then pulls air into the lungs
A.why: Pressure and volume are inversely related, so a larger volume means lower pressure. Lung pressure drops below atmospheric and air flows in.

whyNot.0: Pressure rises when volume DECREASES, as in expiration.
whyNot.1: If lung pressure stayed equal to atmospheric, no air would move.
whyNot.3: Higher pressure inside the lungs pushes air OUT; inflow needs pressure below atmospheric.

A.q: In a healthy adult, how is most of the oxygen in arterial blood carried?
A.why: Nearly all oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin inside red blood cells, as oxyhemoglobin; only a small amount is dissolved in plasma.

whyNot.0: Oxygen dissolves poorly in plasma, so only a small share travels this way.
whyNot.2: Bicarbonate is the main transport form of carbon dioxide, not oxygen.
whyNot.3: Albumin holds water in the blood by osmotic pressure; it is not an oxygen carrier.

B.q: Which statement about quiet expiration at rest is correct?
options: It is active, driven by the internal intercostals
It is passive, driven by elastic recoil
It is active, driven by diaphragm contraction
It is passive, driven by the external intercostals
B.why: At rest, breathing out needs no muscle contraction: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax and the lungs and chest wall recoil.

whyNot.0: The internal intercostals act in FORCED expiration, not quiet expiration at rest.
whyNot.2: Diaphragm contraction drives inspiration; in expiration the diaphragm relaxes.
whyNot.3: The external intercostals lift the ribs during inspiration; they relax during expiration.

B.q: A spinal cord injury damages the phrenic nerves. Which breathing muscle is most directly affected?
B.why: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing.

whyNot.0: The external intercostals help inspiration, but they are not supplied by the phrenic nerve.
whyNot.1: The internal intercostals act in forced expiration and are not supplied by the phrenic nerve.
whyNot.3: Abdominal muscles assist forced expiration; the phrenic nerve does not supply them.

B.q: Which event is an example of internal respiration?
options: O₂ moving from an alveolus into the blood
Air moving into the lungs as the chest expands
A mitochondrion using O₂ to make ATP
O₂ moving from a capillary into a muscle cell
B.why: Internal respiration is gas exchange between systemic capillary blood and body cells: O₂ diffuses into the cells and CO₂ diffuses out.

whyNot.0: Exchange between the alveoli and the blood is external respiration.
whyNot.1: Moving air into the lungs is pulmonary ventilation (breathing).
whyNot.2: Making ATP in mitochondria is cellular respiration, a separate process.

C.q: A patient's spirometry shows: tidal volume 450 mL, IRV 2,900 mL, ERV 1,050 mL, residual volume 1,150 mL. What is the vital capacity?
C.why: Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV = 450 + 2,900 + 1,050 = 4,400 mL. Residual volume is not included.

whyNot.0: 5,550 mL adds the residual volume too: that is total lung capacity, not vital capacity.
whyNot.1: 3,950 mL is IRV + ERV only; the tidal volume was left out.
whyNot.2: 4,500 mL is TV + IRV + RV: residual volume was used in place of ERV.

C.q: Tariq takes a deep breath and then blows out his birthday candles as hard as he can. Which muscles power that forceful blow?
options: Elastic recoil of the lung tissue
C.why: Forced expiration is active: the internal intercostals pull the ribs down and the abdominal muscles push the diaphragm up, squeezing the chest.

whyNot.0: The external intercostals and diaphragm are the muscles of INSPIRATION.
whyNot.2: Elastic recoil alone drives quiet expiration; a forceful blow needs muscle contraction.
whyNot.3: The internal intercostals help, but the diaphragm contracts only to breathe in; in a forced blow the abdominals push it up.

C.q: CO₂ leaving a working muscle enters the blood. In which form, and with the help of which enzyme, is most of it carried to the lungs?
options: Bicarbonate, made by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs
Dissolved CO₂ gas, carried free in the plasma
Bicarbonate, made by surfactant in the alveoli
C.why: Inside red blood cells, carbonic anhydrase speeds CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Most CO₂ then travels as bicarbonate in the plasma; in the lungs the reaction reverses and CO₂ is exhaled.

whyNot.1: Some CO₂ rides on hemoglobin (carbaminohemoglobin), but it is the minority route, and carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate, not carbaminohemoglobin.
whyNot.2: Only a small share of CO₂ travels dissolved in plasma.
whyNot.3: Bicarbonate is the right form, but surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension; it is not an enzyme for CO₂.

reteach.title: Your chest is a syringe
reteach.question: Think of drawing air into a syringe by pulling back the plunger. How does that match breathing in, and what happens when you let go?

blocks.h: Pull the plunger, air rushes in
blocks.body: Pull back a syringe's plunger and the space inside grows. The air inside spreads out, its pressure drops, and outside air rushes in through the tip. Your diaphragm is the plunger: when it contracts and moves down, the chest space grows, lung pressure falls and air flows in. Let go of a springy plunger and it snaps back on its own, pushing air out. That is quiet expiration: elastic recoil, no effort.

blocks.text: The plunger moves AWAY from the tip to draw air in, just as the diaphragm moves DOWN, away from the lungs' top, to inhale. A diaphragm moving up would push air out.

explain.body: Air flows from high to low pressure. Boyle's law: at constant temperature, gas pressure and volume are inversely related. Bigger chest, lower pressure; smaller chest, higher pressure.

test.q: Boyle's law states that, at constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a gas are:
test.why: As volume goes up, pressure goes down, and vice versa: an inverse relationship.

whyNot.0: If they were directly proportional, a bigger chest would raise pressure and push air out.
whyNot.2: Boyle's law describes a simple inverse relationship, not an exponential one.
whyNot.3: Changing one changes the other; that link is the whole basis of breathing.

explain.body: Inspiration is active: the diaphragm (phrenic nerve) contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs. Quiet expiration is passive: the muscles relax and the lungs and chest wall recoil. Forced expiration is active, using the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.

test.q: What mainly drives air out of the lungs during quiet expiration at rest?
options: Elastic recoil of the lungs and chest
test.why: At rest, expiration is passive: relaxed muscles let the lungs and chest wall recoil, shrinking the thorax.

whyNot.0: Internal intercostals contract during forced expiration only when extra effort is needed, not at rest.
whyNot.1: Diaphragm contraction enlarges the chest and causes inspiration.
whyNot.2: Abdominal muscles help forced expiration, not quiet breathing at rest.

explain.body: Tidal volume (about 500 mL), inspiratory reserve, expiratory reserve and residual volume. Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV. Total lung capacity = VC + RV.

test.why: Total lung capacity is everything the lungs can hold: vital capacity plus the residual volume that never leaves.

whyNot.0: Inspiratory reserve volume is already inside vital capacity, so adding it double-counts and misses residual volume.
whyNot.1: This leaves out both reserve volumes.

explain.body: In the lungs (external respiration) O₂ diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and CO₂ from the blood into the alveoli. In the tissues (internal respiration) the directions reverse. Each gas moves from higher to lower partial pressure by simple diffusion, using no ATP.

test.q: What moves oxygen from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillary blood?
test.why: O₂ crosses the thin respiratory membrane by simple diffusion, from its higher partial pressure in the alveoli to its lower partial pressure in the blood.

whyNot.0: No ATP is used: the gas moves down its gradient, not against it.
whyNot.1: Osmosis is the movement of water, not of a dissolved gas.
whyNot.3: Small nonpolar gases pass through the lipid bilayer without carrier proteins.

explain.body: Most O₂ is carried bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells. Most CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate in the plasma, formed by carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells; smaller amounts ride on hemoglobin or travel dissolved.

test.q: Which statement about gas transport in the blood is correct?
options: O₂ mostly as bicarbonate; CO₂ mostly on hemoglobin
O₂ mostly dissolved; CO₂ mostly as bicarbonate
O₂ mostly on hemoglobin; CO₂ mostly dissolved
O₂ mostly on hemoglobin; CO₂ mostly as bicarbonate
test.why: Oxygen travels mainly bound to hemoglobin; carbon dioxide travels mainly as bicarbonate ions in the plasma.

whyNot.0: This swaps the two gases' main forms.
whyNot.1: Only a small share of O₂ is dissolved; most is on hemoglobin.
whyNot.2: Only a small share of CO₂ is dissolved; most is bicarbonate.
